I once successfully negotiated an 80% discount with a hospital. It really wasn't difficult, as their goal is to eventually collect something and close the account. So many people just don't ask and accept the bill as it is presented to them. No insurance company pays full price, and the initial price is elevated as a starting point for negotiation. After you finalize an agreed total, you can set up a payment plan with zero interest. Don't use a credit card or take out a loan to pay medical bills if you can avoid it, because interest will hit you hard.
We need a single payer system in the US so that people don't have to make medical decisions based on cost.

As someone who had Necrotizing Fasciitis as a young child, my mom and I clocked that woman with the rash as having it so fast. I was lucky enough to have a doctor that recognized the symptoms and knew what it was and sent me to the emergency room with a doctor's note. The entire children's hospital ER shut down to give me the care that I needed.

It was a very close call. Flesh Eating Disease in the neck that spread to my armpit. All it took was me coughing into my hand and scratching a chicken pock. My family was told to say goodbye. I was put in a medically induced coma for weeks. I had to have fluid drained from all over my body.

I barely made it, but I did. I had one of THE best plastic surgeons close the wounds on my neck. I still have some scars showing, but I'm proud of them. I was one of the very first children to survive in Canada and they use my case in medical textbooks to teach doctors how to treat Necrotizing Fasciitis :)

comments.text: I feel for the DKA guy. I was experiencing extreme thirst no matter how much water I drank, urinating almost every hour and even walking up the stairs to my apartment left me out of breath, so I went to the ER after my roommate finally convinced me. I was surprised with how swiftly I was admitted to the ICU and with all the questions from the nurses and attending with "are you a diabetic?" and their dubious looks when I said no, because at that time I hadn't been diagnosed. Turns out I have LADA or type 1.5 Diabetes and was in DKA. The doctor scolded me a bit for waiting so long to seek treatment, and told me that if I'd waited another week or so, I might have died. But I was between jobs at the time and didn't have insurance. I was hit with an $86,000.00 bill from the hospital and had to declare bankruptcy, which of course cost more money I didn't have in order to hire an attorney to facilitate my case. Thankfully now, with lifestyle changes and a job that has great insurance I can easily manage things but it took almost 10 years to financially recover. I still can't get a credit card without a security deposit and abhorrent interest.

comments.text: Something that I've always wondered about.  In the forties Sister Kinney developed a second treatment for polio.  Instead of immobilizing the patient's paralyzed limb to prevent pain and spasm, Sister Kinney used hot compresses.  Most of her patients recovered use of the paralyzed limbs while patients given the standard treatment often remained paral;yzed for life.  The medical establishment dismissed her treatment as false diagnoses or fortunate mild cases of polio.  In the sixties, the final edition of the Encyclopedia Britannica before it was trisected in parts sounding like Megalomania, Microcephalia, and Pederasteia noted that the development of effective polio vaccines rendered trhe dispute moot.  If there was clear clinical evidence that Sister Kinney's treatment was worthless, I would think that the medical establishment would have been happy to announce that fact.  The odd dismissal of the controversy "well it doesn't matter anymore" suggests to me that it was Sister Kinney who was right.  Are there any clinical studies on this point?
